scenes.narration: A name made inside a function is local. It exists only while the function runs. A name made outside is global. Python looks for a name locally first, then globally. Think of a hotel. Names inside a room are private. Names in the lobby are shared. A function can read a global name. But if it assigns to that name, Python makes a new local one, unless you say global.

scenes.onScreen: BUG OF THE DAY: using a global before assigning it
scenes.animation: Butter banner drops in with a buzzer; wrong code shakes; the Python error lines appear in tomato; the fix slides in and the terminal turns mint with a ding
scenes.narration: Bug of the Day. We try to add one to the global count. Python says, unbound local error. Cannot access local variable count where it is not associated with a value. Because we assign count in the function, Python treats count as local everywhere in it. The local has no value yet. Declare global count first, and the line works.

shorts.title: Local names
shorts.hook: "A name made inside a function is local."
shorts.script: A name made inside a function is local. It exists only while the function runs, and nothing outside can see it. When the function ends, the name disappears. Think of a hotel room. What happens in the room, stays in the room. Local names keep functions tidy, because they cannot accidentally change names elsewhere in your program. Try it in your own file and watch what happens. Keep coding, says Xecxec!
shorts.caption: Private to the function.

shorts.title: Local first, then global
shorts.hook: "When Python looks for a name, it checks the local names first."
shorts.script: When Python looks for a name, it checks the local names first. If it finds it there, it stops. If not, it checks the global names. So a function can read a global name freely. But if you assign to a name inside a function, Python makes a new local one. The global with the same spelling is hidden, not changed. Keep coding, says Xecxec!
shorts.caption: The lookup order.

shorts.title: The global keyword
shorts.hook: "To change a global name from inside a function, say so first."
shorts.script: To change a global name from inside a function, say so first. The word global, then the name. After that, an assignment in the function changes the global one. It works, but use it sparingly. Code that reaches out and changes global names is hard to follow. Passing values in and returning values out is usually cleaner and safer. Keep coding, says Xecxec!
shorts.caption: Use with care.

shorts.title: Unbound local error
shorts.script: A confusing bug. You write count equals count plus one inside a function. Python says, unbound local error. Because you assign count, Python treats it as local for the whole function, and the local has no value yet. Add the line global count at the top of the function, and it works. Or pass the value in, and return the new one. Keep coding, says Xecxec!
shorts.caption: Declare global.

shorts.hook: "Why did the local variable feel lonely?"
shorts.script: Why did the local variable feel lonely? Nobody outside the function knew its name. Your challenge. Make a global name score, equal to zero. Write a function called bump that adds ten to it, using the global keyword. Call it twice, and print the score. You should see twenty. Then try it without the global line. Post what happens. Keep coding, says Xecxec! Full video: EP 45.
